title: The baptism (Matthew 3:13–17)
hook: Jesus steps into the line of sinners, the sky opens, a voice says beloved

segments.voice: Yesterday, the voice in the desert: John at the river, calling people to metanoia, a turning around. Your line was make straight the way. Did you fill one pothole? Day thirty-two.

Picture the riverbank. A long line of people waiting to go down into the water. Every one of them is there for the same reason: they've done things they regret, and they want to turn around. A tax man. A soldier. A woman who hasn't spoken to her sister in years. Nobody in that line is showing off. And then a carpenter from Nazareth steps into the line. He waits his turn like everybody else. When he reaches the front, John looks at him and stops. He knows who this is. And he tries to refuse. Today: the day Jesus got in line.
screen: `A LINE OF PEOPLE WITH REGRETS.` → `A CARPENTER STEPS INTO LINE.` → `JOHN TRIES TO REFUSE.`

segments.voice: John's words, in the Douay-Rheims: "I ought to be baptized by thee, and comest thou to me?" It's backward, he's saying. You should be baptizing me. Jesus answers that it is fitting, for now, to fulfill all justice, and John lets him come down into the river. Why would Jesus get in the line at all? Christians have asked that for two thousand years. The Church's answer is that he wasn't there for his own sins. He was standing where sinners stand, on purpose, in the water with them. Then the story opens up. As he comes out of the water, Matthew says, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God coming down like a dove and resting on him. And a voice from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Notice when the voice comes. Before a single miracle. Before one sermon, one follower, one healing. He hasn't done anything yet, and he's already beloved. The Church reads this scene as a window onto the Trinity: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice. The feast of the Baptism of the Lord closes the Christmas season, and it's the first of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary. And Catholics hear their own baptism in it. The Catechism teaches that baptism makes a person an adopted child of God. That's why there's holy water at the church door: people dip their fingers and make the sign of the cross on the way in, remembering the water they came through.
screen: `JOHN: YOU SHOULD BAPTIZE ME.` · `HE STANDS WHERE SINNERS STAND.` · `BELOVED, BEFORE HE DOES ANYTHING.` · `HOLY WATER AT THE CHURCH DOOR.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch water and remember you are loved. If you can, get a little water: a glass, a tap, a bowl. Put your fingers in it. Feel how cold or warm it is. If you're Catholic, you might make the sign of the cross, the way people do at the church door. If not, just let the water be water. Now sit, and let one sentence rest on you: loved, before doing anything. Not for your work today. Not for what you'll get right. Just loved. The bell holds the time.
The baptism. Jesus steps into the river with sinners, and a voice from heaven calls him beloved. Today's word.
Your line: you are the beloved. Today, each time you wash your hands, let the water remind you of it. Loved first, before the day's work. Day thirty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Baptism of the Lord as the feast that ends the Christmas season, pray it as the first Luminous Mystery of the rosary, and bless themselves with holy water on entering a church as a reminder of their own baptism.

fork.setup: you're John. the one you've been announcing is standing in your line, waiting to be baptized. what do you do?
options: baptize him quickly, like everyone else.
tell him he should be baptizing you.
announce him to the crowd and step aside.
fork.reveal: John protests: "I ought to be baptized by thee." Jesus says it is fitting for now, and John lets him come.

original.note: Greek: beloved, dearly loved. From agapē, love. The word the voice from heaven uses.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus got baptized to wash off his sins.
what it means: the Church teaches he had no sins to wash. he got in line to stand where sinners stand, and heard he was beloved.
what a scholar hears: Christians read the scene as a picture of the Trinity: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 3:14 and 3:17 given from memory; confirm.
The hook's people in line (a tax man, a soldier) come from Luke 3:12–14, not Matthew; the 'woman estranged from her sister' is illustrative. Confirm this is acceptable as scene-setting.
'He wasn't there for his own sins': Catholic teaching that Jesus was sinless and accepted baptism in solidarity with sinners (CCC 536). Confirm phrasing.
CCC 1265: baptism makes the neophyte an adopted son of God; paraphrased.
Baptism of the Lord ends the Christmas season in the Roman calendar; first Luminous Mystery (John Paul II, Rosarium Virginis Mariae, 2002). Confirm.
Holy water at church doors as a reminder of baptism: describes common practice; confirm.
